items.title: 3.4.1 Formation of sigma and pi bonds

source_refs.note: Topic 3.4.1 (printed 'Formation of Sigma Bond') with the following 'Formation of pi bond', printed pages 59-61 (Figures 3.22 to 3.26), with the Interesting Information box and Quick Check 3.7.

blocks.text: A sigma bond is formed by the linear overlap of two half-filled atomic orbitals on adjacent atoms. The orbitals approach each other on the nuclear axis. Both s and p orbitals can overlap head-on to form sigma bonds.

The ‘s’ orbital of one atom overlaps with the s-orbital of the other to give a bond orbital. This type of overlap occurs during the formation of the H₂ molecule, where each hydrogen atom has a half-filled ‘s’ orbital. After the bond formation, the electrons are paired up and the electron density in this molecule is symmetrical around the two nuclei as in Figure 3.22.

blocks.alt: Two hydrogen s orbitals, each a blue sphere with a nucleus, labelled 's Hydrogen', plus sign between them, and a thick arrow to an oval H2 molecule containing both nuclei. A red arrow from the middle of the oval points to a box reading 'Symmetrical Electron Density'.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.22: Overlap between s orbitals of two hydrogen atoms to form the H2 molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.22).

blocks.text: The s orbital of one atom can overlap with the p orbital of the other to form a covalent bond (σ). For example, in HCl molecule, a half-filled s orbital of hydrogen overlaps with a half-filled p orbital of chlorine as shown in Figure 3.23. The electron density is higher close to the Cl atom due to its higher electronegativity value. This is why HCl is a polar molecule.

blocks.alt: A 1s orbital of a hydrogen atom plus a 3p orbital of a chlorine atom (a dumb-bell). Arrow to 'Overlap starts', where the H sphere touches one lobe of the Cl p orbital. Arrow to 'Hydrogen chloride HCl', drawn with a small lobe on the H side and a larger lobe on the Cl side.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.23: Formation of sigma bond by s-p overlap (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.23).

blocks.text: An example of this type of overlap is the formation of the Cl₂ molecule where ‘p’ orbitals of two chlorine atoms overlap on the nuclear axis. The electron density is symmetrical around the nuclei of the two Cl atoms because both have same value of electronegativity.

blocks.alt: Two 3p orbitals of chlorine atoms, labelled 'Atomic orbitals'. Arrow to the two p orbitals overlapping end to end between the Cl nuclei. Arrow to the Cl2 molecular orbital, a large central lobe between the nuclei with small outer lobes, labelled 'Molecular orbitals' and 'Molecule'.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.24: Overlap of p and p orbitals to form Cl2 molecule according to VBT (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.24).

blocks.text: The H₂S molecule is a non-linear molecule which is formed by the combination of one sulfur and two hydrogen atoms. The two 3p (say 3py and 3pz) orbitals of sulfur containing one electron each can overlap with the 1s orbitals of two hydrogen atoms. A v-shaped molecule is thus formed having a bond angle of 92° as in Fig. 3.25.

blocks.alt: Left: a sulfur atom with axes and its 3p orbitals: two partially filled 3p orbitals (light, outlined) along the vertical and lower-right axes and a filled 3p orbital (dark). Two H atoms sit on the partially filled lobes, with hollow arrows labelled 'Overlap' and a curved double arrow between them labelled 90 degrees. Right: H2S drawn as H-S-H with two green lone-pair lobes on S and the H-S-H angle marked 92 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.25: The formation of H2S molecule by H and S orbitals overlap (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.25).

blocks.title: Interesting Information!
blocks.text: The bond angle in H₂O is 104.5°, whereas in H₂S, it is 92°. This is because the orbitals of S are larger and the lone pair exerts a stronger repulsion.

Consider the formation of a double covalent bond between oxygen atoms (O=O). There are two unpaired electrons on each atom in perpendicular p orbitals (say px and py). The px orbitals on the two oxygen atoms are oriented in such a way that they overlap end-to-end linearly. The linear overlap of the px orbitals gives a σ bond. However, the py orbitals on both atoms are aligned parallel to each other. They overlap in a parallel way so that the two p lobes overlap above the plane of the nuclei and the other two lobes below the plane as shown in Figure 3.26. This results in the formation of π bond. The oxygen atoms are doubly bonded through σ and π bonds.

blocks.alt: Two oxygen nuclei joined by blue px lobes overlapping end to end in the middle, where a dark oval holds a pair of opposite arrows and is labelled 'sigma bond'. Green py lobes stand vertically on each atom along lines labelled y, each upper lobe with an up arrow and labelled Py. Red arcs join the upper lobes and the lower lobes, each labelled 'pi bond'. Below: O=O.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.26: Formation of double bond (sigma and pi) between oxygen atoms (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.26).
